case_analysis.focal_point: Whether the Sixth Amendment’s Confrontation Clause is satisfied when the prosecution introduces a forensic expert’s opinion that is based in part on laboratory test results or statements generated by a non-testifying analyst.
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Smith argues that when the State’s testifying expert relays or depends on testimonial statements/results created by a non-testifying laboratory analyst to prove an element of the offense, the State is effectively introducing the absent analyst’s testimonial assertions for their truth, and the Sixth Amendment requires that analyst to be produced for cross-examination (unless unavailable and previously cross-examined). He contends the State cannot avoid confrontation by presenting the missing analyst’s work through a surrogate expert, because cross-examining the surrogate does not test the competence, methodology, observations, potential errors, or bias of the actual analyst who performed/recorded the critical testing steps.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Arizona argues that the Confrontation Clause is not violated when the State calls a qualified expert who gives an independent opinion based on admissible foundations and/or non-testimonial machine-generated data, even if underlying tests were performed by other laboratory personnel who do not testify. On this view, the testifying expert—not the non-testifying analyst—is the witness against the defendant; the underlying materials are used to explain the basis for the expert’s opinion rather than to introduce the absent analyst’s statements for their truth, and requiring every contributing analyst would be impractical and unnecessary where the testifying expert can be cross-examined about the lab procedures and reliability.
key_precedents: Williams v. Illinois, 567 U.S. 50 (2012) (plurality; fractured decision on surrogate expert/forensic basis testimony)
State v. Pesqueira, 234 Ariz. 470 (Ariz. Ct. App. 2014)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Alito’s administrability objection is the strongest counterpoint, but our precedents already supply a workable, narrow rule: Melendez-Diaz and Bullcoming bar the State from proving an element through case-specific, testimonial forensic assertions of an absent analyst, and calling those assertions “basis” does not change their truth-dependent function at trial. Justice Kavanaugh’s proposed distinction—policing only “conduit” testimony—helps at the margins, but it cannot justify admitting an opinion that is evidentiary only if the jury accepts the non-testifying analyst’s results as true; Justice Kagan is right that the Williams “not for the truth” rationale is unstable in that posture and offers no clear, controlling rule under Marks. A minimal holding that reaffirms Crawford’s core for testimonial, case-specific analyst statements while preserving room for machine-generated data and genuinely independent expert judgments addresses the practical burden without inviting an end-run around confrontation. On that ground, I remain with Petitioner.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Alito’s strongest point is that cross-examining a qualified testifying expert suffices because the underlying lab work is merely a “basis” and not admitted for its truth, and requiring every analyst would be burdensome. But under the Sixth Amendment’s original public meaning and Crawford, the relevant question is whether the State is effectively proving an element through an absent declarant’s testimonial assertions; relabeling those assertions as “basis” cannot erase their truth-dependent function, as Melendez-Diaz and Bullcoming already rejected the surrogate-witness workaround. Justice Roberts is right that Williams provides no administrable, controlling rule under Marks, and the legitimacy-preserving course is to adhere to Crawford’s core: when the testifying expert necessarily conveys case-specific testimonial assertions of a non-testifying analyst to establish guilt, that analyst is a “witness against” the accused who must appear or be previously cross-examined. Practical burdens cannot override a constitutional command, and the Constitution’s text does not permit confrontation to be satisfied by questioning someone who did not make the accusatory testimonial statements.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The strongest point from Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan is the functional-truth concern: if the expert’s opinion matters only if the absent analyst’s result is true, the jury will inevitably treat it that way. But Melendez-Diaz and Bullcoming addressed the State’s use of the non-testifying analyst’s own testimonial certification as substantive evidence; they do not compel a rule that any expert opinion relying on case-specific lab work becomes a conduit, so long as the testifying expert offers an independent judgment and the absent analyst’s assertions are not themselves introduced. Justice Thomas’s insistence that relabeling cannot matter is forceful, yet it risks constitutionalizing a sweeping production requirement that the Sixth Amendment’s text does not clearly demand and that would significantly disrupt routine prosecutions without a commensurate gain where the testifying expert can be fully cross-examined on methods, assumptions, and the reliability of the underlying process. I agree we should police “mere conduit” testimony, but I would not treat all basis reliance on prior lab work as the admission of testimonial hearsay for its truth.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Justice Alito and Justice Kavanaugh’s strongest point—administrability and the availability of cross-examination of a testifying expert—does not answer the core Crawford problem when the expert’s opinion has probative force only if the jury accepts an absent analyst’s case-specific assertions as true. As Justice Kagan explains, the “basis, not for the truth” label becomes a formalism in that posture, because the State is functionally proving an element through untested testimonial statements, precisely what Melendez-Diaz and Bullcoming forbid. Chief Justice Roberts’s narrowing principle addresses the practical concern without hollowing out confrontation: require the actual analyst only when the State conveys testimonial, case-specific observations/results for their truth, while permitting machine-generated data and genuinely independent expert opinions that do not transmit those assertions. Given the real-world stakes for wrongful convictions in forensic cases, I would not constitutionalize a surrogate workaround that leaves defendants unable to test the very assertions doing the decisive work at trial.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Alito’s and Justice Kavanaugh’s strongest point is the administrability/“independent opinion” distinction, but it fails where the expert’s opinion has probative force only if the absent analyst’s case-specific assertions are true—making the jury’s use functionally for truth regardless of a limiting instruction. As Chief Justice Roberts notes, Bullcoming and Melendez-Diaz already reject the surrogate workaround when the State’s proof turns on testimonial forensic assertions prepared for prosecution; cross-examining a reviewer cannot test the original analyst’s observations, competence, or deviations that matter to guilt. Williams does not supply a stable contrary rule (and under Marks provides no controlling rationale), so the workable, coherent line is the one Roberts sketches: require confrontation for testimonial, case-specific analyst statements used to prove an element, while leaving room for machine-generated data and genuinely independent opinions that do not convey those assertions. On a pragmatic textualist view, that approach honors the Sixth Amendment’s command without creating the “every hand in the chain” nightmare Alito warns about.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Alito’s best point is that we traditionally allow experts to rely on others’ work and that the Confrontation Clause is satisfied by cross-examining the witness who gives the opinion at trial. But as Justice Kagan explains, the “not for the truth/basis only” label collapses when the opinion has evidentiary force only if the jury accepts an absent analyst’s case-specific, prosecution-prepared assertions as true—precisely the surrogate maneuver Bullcoming rejected and Melendez-Diaz condemned. Justice Roberts’s narrowing principle answers the administrability concern by distinguishing non-testimonial machine output and genuinely independent judgments from testimonial, case-specific assertions that function as substantive proof of an element. Justice Kavanaugh’s conduit-policing approach is appealing institutionally, but as a textualist/originalist I do not see how the Sixth Amendment’s command can turn on how artfully the State frames the testimony when the prosecution is, in substance, introducing a testimonial witness against the accused without confrontation.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Kagan’s concern about a “surrogate” becoming an end-run around Crawford is the most serious point for Petitioner, and I agree that merely reciting an absent analyst’s case-specific assertions as the decisive predicate for guilt should trigger Melendez-Diaz and Bullcoming. But I read those cases more narrowly—as barring admission of the non-testifying analyst’s own testimonial certification/report as substantive evidence—and they do not, in my view, constitutionalize a categorical rule that every contributing analyst must appear whenever a testifying expert reasonably relies on lab work to form an independent judgment. The administrability and historical practice of expert testimony counsel a workable line policing “conduit” testimony (where the State functionally introduces the absent analyst’s assertions for their truth) while permitting genuinely independent opinions grounded in non-testimonial machine output or background data not itself introduced as the truth of the matter asserted. Williams is fractured as Roberts notes, but that cuts toward a modest, institutionally stabilizing rule focused on preventing surrogate transmission of testimonial statements, not toward expanding Bullcoming into a universal analyst-production requirement.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Alito’s strongest point—that confrontation is satisfied so long as a qualified expert gives an “independent opinion” and the underlying lab work is only basis evidence—fails when, as Justice Kagan emphasizes, the opinion has probative force only if the jury accepts the absent analyst’s case-specific assertions as true. Under Crawford’s text and original public meaning, the “witness against” the accused is the declarant of those testimonial, prosecution-directed assertions, and Melendez-Diaz and Bullcoming directly reject the surrogate-witness workaround that would insulate the actual analyst from cross-examination. Chief Justice Roberts is right that Williams supplies no controlling rule under Marks; in that vacuum, fidelity to our clearer holdings and an administrable line is to require confrontation for testimonial, case-specific forensic statements used to prove an element, while leaving room for machine-generated data and genuinely independent expert judgments not transmitting an absent analyst’s assertions. Justice Kavanaugh’s administrability concerns do not justify converting a truth-dependent conveyance of testimonial assertions into a mere “basis” label, which would let form defeat the Clause’s substance.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Alito’s administrability point has force, and Justice Kavanaugh is right to worry about “conduit” policing rather than a universal analyst-production rule. But as Justice Kagan emphasizes, the “basis, not for truth” distinction collapses when the expert’s opinion has probative value only if the jury accepts the absent analyst’s case-specific results as true—making that analyst functionally a witness against the accused under Crawford, Melendez-Diaz, and Bullcoming. Chief Justice Roberts’s narrowing principle answers the workload concern without draining confrontation of meaning: allow machine-generated output and genuinely independent opinions, but require confrontation when the State proves an element by transmitting testimonial, case-specific assertions from a non-testifying analyst. Under a pragmatic fairness lens, cross-examining a surrogate cannot test the original analyst’s competence, deviations, or mistakes, and the real-world risk of error in forensic evidence outweighs the efficiency gains in this core category.

John Roberts.reasoning: The Confrontation Clause requires that testimonial statements offered for their truth be subject to cross-examination, and the State may not evade that requirement by presenting a surrogate expert to convey or functionally introduce an absent analyst’s case-specific assertions. Williams v. Illinois produced no controlling majority under Marks, leaving lower courts divided, and in that uncertainty the narrowest, legitimacy-preserving course is to apply the core Crawford principle: if the expert’s opinion depends on and communicates testimonial lab results/observations of a non-testifying analyst to prove an element, the analyst is a “witness against” the accused who must be produced (absent unavailability plus prior cross-examination). This rule can be applied narrowly to testimonial, case-specific analyst statements, while permitting reliance on non-testimonial machine-generated data and truly independent expert opinions that do not relay the absent analyst’s assertions for their truth. U.S. Const. amend. VI thus is not satisfied where the prosecution’s proof turns on testimonial lab work of a non-testifying analyst presented through a substitute.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The Sixth Amendment guarantees the accused the right “to be confronted with the witnesses against him,” and under its original public meaning that includes the actual declarant whose testimonial assertions the State offers to prove guilt. Under Crawford v. Washington, testimonial statements may not be introduced unless the witness is unavailable and the defendant had a prior opportunity to cross-examine; this rule applies to forensic laboratory certifications and reports prepared for prosecution. Melendez-Diaz v. Massachusetts and Bullcoming v. New Mexico confirm that the State may not satisfy confrontation by introducing an absent analyst’s testimonial lab results through a surrogate expert, because the surrogate is not the witness who made the critical assertions and cannot be cross-examined about the original analyst’s observations and potential errors. Accordingly, when the testifying expert’s opinion depends on and effectively conveys the non-testifying analyst’s testimonial statements for their truth, the Confrontation Clause is violated absent prior cross-examination.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The Confrontation Clause, U.S. Const. amend. VI, is satisfied when the prosecution presents a qualified expert who gives an independent opinion and is subject to full cross-examination, even if that opinion rests in part on laboratory work performed by non-testifying personnel. Williams v. Illinois, 567 U.S. 50 (2012), though fractured, supports the proposition that an expert’s reliance on underlying lab results does not necessarily amount to introducing those statements for their truth when they are used to explain the basis of the expert’s opinion rather than as a substitute for live testimony. Requiring every analyst who touched a sample to testify would impose severe and unnecessary burdens on prosecutions and laboratories, with little added reliability where the testifying expert can be cross-examined about procedures, potential errors, and the grounds for the opinion. So long as the testifying expert is not a mere conduit for an absent analyst’s conclusions, confrontation is met by confronting the witness who actually testifies against the defendant.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: When the State proves an element of the offense by presenting an expert opinion that necessarily conveys, for its truth, the substantive results or assertions of a non-testifying analyst, the defendant is denied the Sixth Amendment right "to be confronted with the witnesses against him." Melendez-Diaz held that forensic certificates prepared for prosecution are testimonial and cannot substitute for live testimony, and Bullcoming likewise rejected the use of a surrogate scientist to introduce a testimonial certification created by an absent analyst. Cross-examining a "surrogate" expert cannot meaningfully probe the absent analyst’s observations, competence, and potential errors—concerns with especially grave practical consequences for criminal defendants facing the weight juries often place on forensic evidence. The Confrontation Clause therefore requires the State to produce the analyst who made the testimonial statements/results (or show unavailability plus a prior opportunity for cross-examination).

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The Confrontation Clause requires that when the State proves an element of the offense through testimonial forensic assertions made by a non-testifying analyst, the defendant must have the opportunity to cross-examine that analyst, and the State cannot avoid that obligation by channeling the analyst’s work through a “surrogate” expert. Although Williams v. Illinois produced no clear controlling rule under Marks, the plurality’s “not for the truth” rationale is unworkable in practice because juries necessarily treat the absent analyst’s reported results as true when they supply the factual predicate for the expert’s opinion—precisely the kind of end-run the Confrontation Clause forbids. As in my Williams dissent, allowing basis testimony to convey an absent analyst’s critical observations and conclusions with a “wink and a nod” would drain confrontation of meaning and reduce cross-examination to testing only the surrogate’s review rather than the actual testing, potential error, or bias. The Sixth Amendment therefore is not satisfied here unless the State produces the analyst who generated the testimonial statements/results (or shows unavailability plus a prior opportunity for cross-examination).

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The Sixth Amendment guarantees the accused the right “to be confronted with the witnesses against him,” and under Crawford v. Washington the State may not introduce testimonial statements of an absent witness unless the witness is unavailable and the defendant had a prior opportunity for cross-examination. Laboratory notes or reports prepared for the primary purpose of establishing facts for use in a criminal prosecution are testimonial, and this Court has held in Melendez-Diaz and Bullcoming that the prosecution may not evade confrontation by presenting such forensic assertions through a surrogate analyst. When the testifying expert’s opinion depends in part on those testimonial assertions to prove an element of the offense, the absent analyst is effectively a witness against the accused, and cross-examining only the surrogate does not satisfy the Confrontation Clause. Whatever uncertainty remains after the fractured Williams decision, Bullcoming’s rule squarely rejects a “surrogate testimony” workaround for testimonial forensic reports.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The Confrontation Clause bars admission of testimonial statements from a non-testifying witness offered for their truth unless the witness is unavailable and previously cross-examined. U.S. Const. amend. VI; Crawford v. Washington. But where the State presents a qualified expert who testifies to his own independent opinion, and the underlying material is used only as the basis for that opinion (not introduced for its truth), the defendant confronts the actual “witness against him” through cross-examination of the testifying expert, consistent with the fractured guidance in Williams v. Illinois and the Court’s practical approach to expert-basis testimony. Requiring every contributing analyst to testify would be difficult to administer in routine forensic cases and is not compelled absent the State’s introduction of the absent analyst’s testimonial assertions as substantive evidence.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The Sixth Amendment bars admission of testimonial statements from a non-testifying witness unless the witness is unavailable and the defendant had a prior opportunity to cross-examine. Crawford v. Washington, 541 U.S. 36 (2004). Under Melendez-Diaz v. Massachusetts, 557 U.S. 305 (2009), and Bullcoming v. New Mexico, 564 U.S. 647 (2011), forensic reports or recorded analytical assertions prepared for use in prosecution are testimonial, and the State may not satisfy confrontation by calling a surrogate expert who did not perform or observe the critical testing steps. Where the testifying expert’s opinion necessarily conveys or depends on the absent analyst’s testimonial assertions to prove an element of the offense, the absent analyst is the relevant “witness against” the accused, and confrontation is required.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The Confrontation Clause bars the State from proving an element of the offense by introducing testimonial forensic assertions created for prosecution through a surrogate witness, unless the original analyst is unavailable and was previously subject to cross-examination. Under Melendez-Diaz v. Massachusetts and Bullcoming v. New Mexico, laboratory reports or certified statements prepared to establish a fact at trial are testimonial, and calling a different expert who did not perform or observe the critical testing does not supply the constitutionally required opportunity to probe the actual analyst’s observations, competence, and potential errors. Although Williams v. Illinois is fractured, it does not authorize using a testifying expert as a conduit for an absent analyst’s testimonial notes/report when the State relies on those assertions for their truth. As a matter of procedural fairness and practical consequences in criminal cases, the Sixth Amendment (U.S. Const. amend. VI) requires confrontation of the analyst whose testimonial work is being used against the accused.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether the Sixth Amendment’s Confrontation Clause allows the prosecution to introduce the substance of a non-testifying lab analyst’s testimonial assertions through a testifying expert who relied on the analyst’s lab work/data to form an opinion.
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Smith argues that when the State’s expert conveys (explicitly or effectively) the results and conclusions of a non-testifying forensic analyst to prove an element of the offense, the State is introducing testimonial statements without producing the actual declarant for cross-examination. In Smith’s view, the Confrontation Clause is not satisfied by calling a surrogate expert who neither performed nor observed the underlying testing and who can only repeat or adopt another analyst’s assertions. He contends cross-examination must be available against the analyst(s) who actually generated the testimonial lab results, particularly where the lab work is prepared for prosecution and is functionally an out-of-court accusation.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Arizona argues that the Confrontation Clause is satisfied when a qualified expert appears, is sworn, and is cross-examined, even if the expert’s opinion is based in part on data generated by other analysts. In the State’s view, the testifying expert offers an independent opinion rather than serving as a conduit for another analyst’s testimonial statements; to the extent underlying lab materials are referenced, they are used as the basis for the expert’s opinion and not admitted for their truth in a way that triggers confrontation. Arizona also relies on state precedent applying this approach and on the view that requiring every participating analyst to testify would be impractical and unnecessary where the expert can explain methods, interpret machine-generated data, and be cross-examined about reliability and conclusions.
key_precedents: Williams v. Illinois, 567 U.S. 50 (2012) (plurality decision; cited as 132 S. Ct. 2221)
State v. Pesqueira, 234 Ariz. 470 (Ariz. Ct. App. 2014)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Alito’s administrability point—that we should not effectively require every technician in the chain to testify—remains the strongest argument on the other side, and it counsels against an overbroad rule. But his proposed conduit/recitation line is unstable in practice: as Justice Kagan and Justice Sotomayor stress, juries necessarily credit the testifying expert only by accepting the absent analyst’s case-specific assertions about what was done and what the results mean, which makes the absent analyst a functional “witness against” the accused under Melendez-Diaz and Bullcoming. Justice Thomas’s emphasis on testimonial formality reinforces the narrow route that best preserves our precedents and institutional legitimacy: permit reliance on genuinely non-testimonial, machine-generated, or background data, but forbid the prosecution from conveying the substance of an absent analyst’s testimonial conclusions to prove an element without confrontation. Williams’s fractured rationale cannot bear the weight of expanding a “basis” fiction that would dilute Crawford’s core protection against trial by affidavit.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Alito’s strongest point is the asserted distinction between admitting an absent analyst’s testimonial statement “for its truth” and allowing an expert to give an “independent opinion” based on underlying materials; but as Justice Roberts notes, that line collapses when the expert’s testimony effectively conveys the absent analyst’s accusatory, case-specific conclusions to prove an element of the offense. Under the Sixth Amendment’s text and Crawford’s original-meaning rule, a prosecution-prepared forensic certification is a “witness against” the accused, and Melendez-Diaz and Bullcoming forbid substituting cross-examination of a proxy for confrontation of the actual declarant. Williams v. Illinois, as Justice Kagan observes, provides no controlling rationale to dilute those holdings; to the extent it matters, it only reinforces that courts should not accept “not for the truth” fictions when the jury must rely on the absent analyst’s assertions. I therefore remain persuaded that the Constitution requires production of the analyst (or prior cross-examination with unavailability) when the State functionally places her testimonial assertions before the jury.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: I take Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Kagan’s conduit concern seriously: “basis” testimony cannot be permitted to smuggle an absent analyst’s accusatory, case-specific conclusions to the jury for their truth. But Bullcoming is best read to bar true surrogate testimony that introduces or effectively recites the absent analyst’s formalized certification, not to impose a categorical requirement that the particular technician who performed each step must appear whenever a qualified expert can independently interpret non-testimonial, machine-generated outputs and standard procedures. Justice Thomas’s focus on formality reinforces the limiting principle I would adopt: exclude the absent analyst’s formal testimonial assertions themselves, while allowing a testifying expert’s own opinion so long as the prosecution does not introduce, quote, or meaningfully parrot the absent analyst’s conclusions as the proof of an element. The petitioner-side rule risks collapsing into an impractical “produce everyone” regime in routine cases and goes beyond what Crawford/Melendez-Diaz/Bullcoming require when the State does not place the absent analyst’s testimonial statement before the jury as such.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Justice Alito’s administrability concern—that we not require every technician in the chain—matters, but it does not justify allowing the prosecution to prove an element by transmitting an absent analyst’s case-specific assertions through a purportedly “independent” expert opinion. As the Chief Justice and Justice Kagan emphasize, in the forensic setting the jury can credit the opinion only by accepting the non-testifying analyst’s accuracy and protocol compliance, so the “not for the truth/basis” label becomes a real-world fiction and an end-run around Melendez-Diaz and Bullcoming. Justice Thomas’s focus on testimonial formality may help identify which statements trigger confrontation, but once the State functionally places a prosecution-prepared accusatory lab conclusion before the jury, cross-examining a proxy does not protect defendants—especially the vulnerable—from documented forensic error and misconduct. A narrow rule barring conduit testimony while allowing reliance on genuinely non-testimonial, machine-generated, or background data addresses Alito’s practical point without sacrificing the Sixth Amendment’s core guarantee of fairness.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Alito’s administrability point—that we should distinguish admitting an absent analyst’s statement for its truth from allowing a live expert’s independent opinion—has force in the abstract, and I agree we should not constitutionalize a rule that drags every technician in the chain into court. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Sotomayor emphasize, that line collapses when the expert’s opinion can be credited only if the jury accepts the absent analyst’s case-specific, prosecution-prepared conclusions (and implied protocol compliance) as true; that is the “conduit” problem condemned in Bullcoming and consistent with Melendez-Diaz. Williams’s fractured reasoning does not supply a stable, precedent-coherent safe harbor for “basis” fictions, so the most workable textual rule is to permit reliance on genuinely non-testimonial or machine-generated/background data while forbidding the State from conveying an absent analyst’s testimonial accusatory assertions to prove an element without confrontation. Alito’s proposed ‘no meaningful parroting’ standard is too indeterminate in application and invites exactly the end-run our Confrontation Clause cases have tried to prevent.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Alito’s administrability concern—that we not require every technician in the chain—has force, but his proposed “independent opinion” line fails where the expert’s conclusion depends on the truth of an absent analyst’s case-specific assertions and the jury must accept those assertions to convict; that is surrogate testimony in substance, which Bullcoming and Melendez-Diaz forbid. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan explain, a workable, precedent-faithful boundary exists: experts may rely on genuinely non-testimonial, machine-generated, or general background data, but the State may not transmit the substance of a non-testifying analyst’s accusatory conclusions to prove an element. Justice Thomas’s emphasis on testimonial formality helps identify the core class of statements at issue (prosecution-prepared forensic certifications), but even absent rigid formality the Sixth Amendment’s text—“witnesses against him”—is not satisfied by cross-examining a proxy when the real declarant’s assertions are doing the inculpatory work. Williams’s fractured decision cannot be treated as silently overruling the clearer Crawford-line forensic cases, so I remain with petitioner under a principled, originalist application of confrontation.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Alito’s administrability point—that we should not require every technician in the chain to appear—has real force, and I agree with his focus on preventing a categorical “everyone must testify” rule. But as the Chief Justice emphasizes, the constitutional violation occurs when the State proves an element by having a testifying expert functionally transmit an absent analyst’s case-specific, prosecution-prepared conclusions to the jury; that is precisely the surrogate problem condemned in Melendez-Diaz and Bullcoming, and Williams supplies no controlling rationale to authorize that end-run through “basis” testimony. Justice Thomas’s formality emphasis also reinforces that when the absent analyst’s assertions are formalized and accusatory, they are testimonial and confrontation is required. The workable, legitimacy-preserving line is to allow expert reliance on genuinely non-testimonial or machine-generated data while barring the conveyance/adoption of an absent analyst’s testimonial conclusions absent confrontation.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Alito’s administrability point—allowing a testifying expert’s “independent opinion” while excluding the absent analyst’s formal assertions—does not solve the Confrontation Clause problem when the opinion’s persuasive force depends on the jury accepting the absent analyst’s case-specific conclusions as true. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, that is functionally the admission of a testimonial accusation through a surrogate, which Crawford, Melendez-Diaz, and Bullcoming forbid; cross-examining the proxy is not confrontation of the actual “witness against” the accused. Justice Thomas’s focus on formality may help identify the core category of testimonial lab certifications, but even without a formal certificate the Clause is violated when the State conveys the substance of prosecution-prepared, accusatory assertions needed to prove an element. Williams provides no controlling rationale to authorize a “basis” fiction that effectively reintroduces those assertions for their truth, so I would hold to a narrow, workable line: experts may rely on genuinely non-testimonial or machine-generated data, but may not transmit an absent analyst’s testimonial conclusions absent confrontation.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Alito’s administrability concern about not requiring “every technician in the chain” is serious, but it does not justify allowing the State to prove an element by transmitting an absent analyst’s case-specific accusatory conclusions through an “independent opinion” label—because in practice the jury must accept the absent analyst’s assertions as true to credit the opinion, recreating the surrogate-testimony problem Bullcoming condemned. Chief Justice Roberts’s proposed boundary (experts may rely on truly non-testimonial or machine-generated data, but may not convey testimonial conclusions of a non-testifying analyst) squarely addresses Alito’s practical point while preserving Crawford/Melendez-Diaz’s procedural safeguard against trial by affidavit. Williams’s fractured opinions, as Justice Kagan emphasizes, provide no stable narrowing rule that would legitimize “basis” fictions when the prosecution’s evidentiary theory functionally depends on the absent declarant’s truthfulness. Under a pragmatic fairness lens, the marginal burden of producing the critical analyst is outweighed by the real-world risk of insulating forensic error or misconduct from meaningful cross-examination.

John Roberts.reasoning: The Confrontation Clause guarantees the accused the right “to be confronted with the witnesses against him,” U.S. Const. amend. VI, and that right is not satisfied when the prosecution proves an element by transmitting the substance of a non-testifying analyst’s testimonial conclusions through a surrogate expert. Given Williams v. Illinois’s fractured reasoning and the ensuing confusion, the narrowest, precedent-respecting course is to hold that when an expert’s testimony effectively conveys an absent analyst’s accusatory, prosecution-prepared assertions for their truth, the analyst is a “witness against” the defendant and must be produced for cross-examination. This rule preserves institutional legitimacy by providing a clear, administrable boundary—experts may give independent opinions from non-testimonial or machine-generated data, but the State may not introduce testimonial lab assertions without the declarant. Requiring confrontation in that circumstance aligns with the Court’s post-Crawford approach distinguishing testimonial statements from other bases of expert reliance, while avoiding an overbroad mandate that every technician in a chain must appear.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The Sixth Amendment guarantees the accused the right “to be confronted with the witnesses against him,” and under Crawford v. Washington testimonial statements may be admitted only if the declarant is unavailable and the defendant previously had an opportunity for cross-examination. Forensic lab reports and related analyst certifications prepared for use in a criminal prosecution are testimonial, so the State may not introduce their substance through a surrogate witness who neither performed nor observed the testing, as held in Melendez-Diaz v. Massachusetts and Bullcoming v. New Mexico. Allowing a testifying expert to convey or functionally adopt a non-testifying analyst’s conclusions to prove an element of the offense would evade the Confrontation Clause’s text and original public meaning by substituting cross-examination of the real accuser with cross-examination of a proxy. Williams v. Illinois provides no controlling basis to dilute Crawford’s rule, and the Constitution requires the actual analyst (or a prior cross-examined, unavailable declarant) when the prosecution offers the analyst’s testimonial assertions for their truth.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The Sixth Amendment bars admitting testimonial statements of a non-testifying analyst for their truth, but it does not forbid a qualified expert from giving an independent opinion based on underlying lab data not itself introduced as substantive evidence. Bullcoming v. New Mexico, 564 U.S. 647 (2011), is best read to prohibit true “surrogate” testimony that merely transmits a certified report’s accusatory assertions, not to require every contributing technician to appear whenever a testifying expert can interpret machine-generated data and explain methodology under cross-examination. Williams v. Illinois, 567 U.S. 50 (2012), though fractured, supports the distinction between admitting an out-of-court testimonial assertion for its truth and permitting an expert to rely on materials as the basis for an opinion, and the practical consequences of petitioner’s rule would unduly burden prosecutions with marginal gains in reliability. So long as the State’s witness is not used as a conduit to introduce the absent analyst’s testimonial conclusions, the Confrontation Clause is satisfied by in-court testimony and cross-examination of the expert.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The Confrontation Clause bars the State from proving an element of the offense by conveying a non-testifying analyst’s testimonial assertions through a surrogate expert, because the defendant is entitled to cross-examine the actual declarant whose statements function as an out-of-court accusation. Under Crawford and its forensic-line cases, lab certifications prepared for prosecution are testimonial, and Bullcoming v. New Mexico makes clear that calling an analyst who neither performed nor observed the testing does not satisfy the Sixth Amendment when that witness effectively transmits the absent analyst’s results and conclusions. Whatever room Williams v. Illinois left in its fractured opinions cannot override the straightforward rule of Melendez-Diaz and Bullcoming when the jury is asked to accept the absent analyst’s assertions for their truth. Practical concerns can be addressed through notice-and-demand procedures, but fairness—especially for defendants facing unreliable or error-prone forensic practices—requires live confrontation of the analyst who did the work.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The Confrontation Clause guarantees the accused the right “to be confronted with the witnesses against him,” U.S. Const. amend. VI, and that protection is undermined when the prosecution effectively introduces an absent analyst’s accusatory, prosecution-prepared forensic conclusions through a testifying expert who did not perform or observe the testing. Williams v. Illinois provides no controlling majority rationale, but it underscores the surrogate-testimony problem: four Justices rejected the “not for the truth” characterization as a fiction when the jury must accept the underlying analyst’s assertions to credit the expert’s opinion, and Justice Thomas would bar admission when the absent analyst’s statements are formalized and testimonial. A workable, middle-ground rule is to allow experts to rely on non-testimonial, machine-generated or background data, but to forbid conveying the substance of a non-testifying analyst’s testimonial conclusions to prove an element of the offense absent prior cross-examination or production of that analyst. That approach promotes administrability and coherence while preserving the core confrontation right against the real accuser in the lab-report context.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The Confrontation Clause guarantees the accused the right “to be confronted with the witnesses against him,” and under Crawford v. Washington the State may not introduce testimonial statements of an absent witness unless the witness is unavailable and the defendant had a prior opportunity for cross-examination. Forensic lab conclusions prepared for use in prosecution are testimonial, and this Court held in Melendez-Diaz v. Massachusetts and Bullcoming v. New Mexico that the prosecution cannot satisfy confrontation by presenting a surrogate who did not perform or observe the testing while effectively relaying the absent analyst’s assertions. Allowing a testifying expert to convey the substance of a non-testifying analyst’s accusatory, case-specific lab conclusions would evade the Sixth Amendment’s text and the separation-of-powers limits it imposes on courts and prosecutors alike. Williams v. Illinois lacks a controlling rationale and cannot be read to overrule Melendez-Diaz and Bullcoming’s core holding that the actual analyst-witness must be subject to cross-examination when her testimonial assertions are used to prove an element of the offense.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Under the Sixth Amendment’s Confrontation Clause, the prosecution may not introduce testimonial forensic accusations through a “surrogate” expert when the substance of the non-testifying analyst’s conclusions is effectively conveyed to prove an element of the offense. Crawford v. Washington and Melendez-Diaz v. Massachusetts make clear that testimonial lab certifications prepared for prosecution are subject to confrontation, and Bullcoming v. New Mexico rejects substituting a different analyst who neither performed nor observed the critical testing. Williams v. Illinois did not produce a controlling rationale that authorizes admitting testimonial lab conclusions via expert “basis” testimony, and as a practical, workable rule consistent with history and precedent, the State must present the actual analyst (or avoid introducing the analyst’s testimonial assertions for their truth).

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The Confrontation Clause provides that, “[i]n all criminal prosecutions, the accused shall enjoy the right … to be confronted with the witnesses against him,” U.S. Const. amend. VI, and under Crawford v. Washington testimonial statements may be introduced only if the declarant is unavailable and the defendant had a prior opportunity for cross-examination. Where the prosecution uses a testifying expert to convey the substance of a non-testifying analyst’s lab conclusions prepared for prosecution, the analyst is a “witness against” the accused and the State is effectively introducing testimonial assertions without confrontation. Bullcoming v. New Mexico holds that surrogate testimony cannot substitute for cross-examining the analyst who performed (or observed) the testing when the State is using that analyst’s certified results and procedures to prove an element of the offense. Williams v. Illinois does not clearly authorize the State’s approach given its fractured rationale, and methodological consistency with Crawford/Melendez-Diaz/Bullcoming counsels requiring confrontation of the actual analyst when her testimonial assertions are functionally placed before the jury for their truth.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The Confrontation Clause bars the State from proving an element of the offense by transmitting to the jury the substance of a non-testifying analyst’s testimonial assertions through a surrogate expert, because the accused is entitled to cross-examine the actual declarant whose out-of-court accusatory statement is offered for its truth. Under Melendez-Diaz v. Massachusetts, forensic reports prepared for prosecution are testimonial, and under Bullcoming v. New Mexico the State may not introduce such a testimonial certification through an analyst who neither performed nor observed the testing. Arizona’s framing of the testimony as an “independent opinion” cannot cure a confrontation problem when, in practical effect, the expert functions as a conduit for the absent analyst’s conclusions that were generated for evidentiary use. Requiring confrontation here promotes procedural fairness and reliable factfinding in criminal cases, consistent with the Sixth Amendment’s core protection against trial by affidavit.
